segments.text: Have you ever known the answer, but you couldn't say it in English?
Have you ever understood a video, but you missed some key words?
Someone asks you a question in English, and your mind goes completely blank.
Ugh, that feels terrible, right?
Well, you're not alone.
This happens to almost every English learner, and today we're going to fix it.
So, why does this happen?
The main reason is simple.
You're translating in your head.
You hear English, you translate it to your language, you think of a response in your language, then you translate it back to English.
That takes too much
time.
Let me share a story with you.
I remember this happened to me when I was learning Spanish.
I was in a small coffee shop in Madrid.
The waiter came to my table and asked me a simple question.
"What would you like to drink?"
Easy, right?
But my mind went blank.
I knew the words. I'd studied them many times.
But my brain was working like a computer with a slow internet connection.
First, I translated his question into my language.
Then, I thought of my answer in my language.
Then, I tried to translate that into Spanish.
And then, I opened my mouth.
But nothing came out.
The waiter was waiting.
I felt my face getting hot.
My heart was beating fast.
I finally said, "Um coffee, please."
But I made a grammar mistake.
The waiter smiled and said, "Un café, por supuesto."
He was kind, but I felt so embarrassed.
I knew the words.
I had practiced.
But my brain was translating everything.
That was my problem.
And if you're watching this video, maybe that's your problem, too.
Here's what I discovered.
When you translate in your head, you're not really learning English.
You're just learning to
translate.
And that's a big difference.
Think about this.
When you speak your native language, do you think about grammar rules?
No.
Do you translate from another language?
No.
The words just come out naturally.
That's because you think in your language.
Your brain connects ideas directly to words.
You don't go through a translation process.
So, to speak English naturally, you need to think in English.
Not translate.
Think.
That is the secret.
So, how can you start thinking in English?
Here are three simple things you can do today.
Number one, name things around you.
This is the easiest way to start.
Look around you right now.
What do you see?
A phone, a chair, a window, a cup.
Say these words in English.
But, don't just say them.
Look at the object and think the word in English.
Don't translate.
Just connect the image to the English word.
When you see a door, think door.
When you see a book, think book.
Do this every day.
Do it when you wake up.
Do it when you're walking.
Do it when you're cooking.
Soon, these words will become automatic.
You won't need to translate.
Your brain will connect the object to the English word directly.
Why does this work?
Because you're creating a direct connection.
You're training your brain to think in English.
You're not using your native language as You're building a new bridge directly to English.
Number two, think in simple sentences.
Once you're comfortable with words, move to sentences.
Describe what you're doing.
In your head, say, "I am making coffee.
I am opening the door.
I am sitting on the chair."
Again, don't translate.
Just think it in English.
If you don't know a word, don't stop.
Describe it another way.
"I am making a hot drink.
I am using the thing to open the door.
I am sitting on the furniture."
This is called circumlocution, and it's a powerful tool.
It helps you keep thinking in English without stopping.
You can do this anytime.
When you're in the shower, think, "I am washing my hair."
When you're eating, think, "This food is delicious."
When you're walking, think, "It is a sunny day."
Start with simple sentences, then make them more complex.
"I am making coffee because I feel tired.
I am opening the door to go outside.
I am sitting on the chair and reading a book."
This will train your brain to form sentences naturally.
Number three, talk to yourself in English.
This is my favorite technique.
Talk to yourself.
Yes, I'm serious.
You can do it quietly in your head, or you can speak out loud when you're alone.
Plan your day in English.
"Today, I need to go to the supermarket.
I want to buy milk, bread, and eggs.
After that, I will call my friend."
Narrate your activities.
"I am brushing my teeth now.
I need to send that email.
I should start cooking dinner."
Ask yourself questions.
"What should I eat for lunch?
Did I lock the door?
Do I have time to watch a movie?
And then answer them in English.
Maybe I'll eat pasta.
Yes, I locked the door.
No, I don't have time.
Why does this work?
Because you're practicing real communication.
You're not just studying grammar.
You're using English to think about your life.
This makes English part of your daily routine.
It stops being a subject you study.
It becomes a tool you use.
And when something is a tool, you don't translate it.
You just use it.
Try these three things.
Start today.
Name things around you.
Think in simple sentences.
Talk to yourself in English.
Do this for 1 week and you will see a difference.
Remember, thinking in English is a skill, and like any skill, it takes time.
You will make mistakes.
That's okay.
That's how you learn.
Don't be afraid of mistakes.
Be afraid of not trying.
Start small.
Be consistent and celebrate your progress.
Now, I have a question for you.
What is one thing you see around you right now?
Write it in English in the comments below.
Just one word.
Let's practice together.
I'll read your comments and cheer for you.
You can do this.
I believe in you.
Keep going.
See you in the next video.
Take care.
